title: Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
author: Zhanran, compiler and annotator
excerpt: Thought after thought continuing to the end of life; rousing the mind and restraining oneself, day and night never ceasing.

inline.s: Single-minded recitation of the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth.
Thought after thought continuing to the end of life,
rousing the mind and restraining oneself, day and night never ceasing.
Master Shandao is an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha; his words are the words of Amitabha Buddha.
Concerning how to attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss,
Master Shandao gave extremely important teachings, and this is Shandao's Pure Land teaching. It is now annotated as follows:

single-minded recitation of the name.” This teaching, recorded in the Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra, is an important teaching by Master Shandao on how to practice the Pure Land school
— for on how to practice (some today even publicly proclaim that Master Shandao held that reciting the name surely leads to rebirth, and that reciting with a scattered mind is acceptable)
In his teaching, Master Shandao strongly emphasized
single-mindedness:
whether in reciting sutras, in contemplation, in worship of the Buddha, in reciting the name, or in praise and offerings,
all must be done with
single-mindedness,
for this is the
key to correct practice!
And among the many practices,
single-minded recitation of the name
is the most important and most supreme of all great methods.
“Single-minded recitation of the name, never relinquishing it thought after thought”
— this is the
heart and marrow
of Master Shandao's Pure Land teaching.
Master Shandao says:

“There are two kinds of practice: the first is correct practice; the second is mixed practice. By ‘correct practice’ is meant practicing exclusively in accordance with the scriptures on rebirth—this is called correct practice. What is this? With
single-minded attention
exclusively recite this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, the Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so on;
with single-minded attention
exclusively contemplate, reflect upon, and recollect the two kinds of adornment of that land. If one worships, then
with single-minded attention
exclusively worship that Buddha; if one recites aloud, then
with single-minded attention
exclusively recite that Buddha; if one praises and makes offerings, then
with single-minded attention
exclusively praise and make offerings.
This is called correct practice.
(The Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra)
Single-mindedness:
It means being pure and unmixed.
Single-mindedness
means the mind continuing thought after thought, with no other thoughts intruding—that is, without scattered thoughts.
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, in the Treatise on Rebirth, says:
“O World-Honored One, I
single-mindedly
take refuge in the Tathagata of Unobstructed Light throughout the ten directions
(that is, Amitabha Buddha)
, desiring rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Master Tanluan, in the Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, explains:
single-mindedly’
— this is the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu's own words of self-admonition. It says: recollecting the Tathagata of Unobstructed Light, and desiring rebirth in the Land of Bliss,
the mind continues thought after thought, with no other thought intruding.
Therefore, ‘single-mindedness’ means the mind continuing thought after thought, with no other thought intruding.
[The Tathagata of Unobstructed Light] One of the twelve different names of Amitabha Buddha.
Master Zhiyi says:
“If with the mind one keeps recollecting,
thought after thought continuing
with no other thought interrupting
(that is, not interrupted by other thoughts)
therefore it is called single-minded
(The Commentary on the Meaning of Avalokitesvara)
Single-mindedness means concentrating the mind on one thing, without a second thought.
It is also what Master Yongming, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, calls
“no differing thoughts
(that is, no other thoughts)
Master Yongming says:
“When walking the path
(practicing walking meditation)
and paying respects, or at the time of reciting the Buddha's name and making vows, with earnest and utmost sincerity,
free of all differing thoughts,
as one about to be executed, or confined in a prison
(bi
bi
— prison means a jail)
, pursued by enemies and thieves, beset by water and fire,
single-mindedly

seeking deliverance, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize non-arising, to broadly save all sentient beings, to uphold and carry forward the Three Jewels, and to vow to repay the four kinds of kindness. With sincerity such as this, one's efforts will surely not be wasted.”

(Translation: At the time of walking meditation and paying respects, and at the time of reciting the Buddha's name and making vows, be earnest and devout, free of scattered thoughts—as one facing execution, as one imprisoned, as one pursued by enemies and thieves, as one beset by water and fire—and, urgently and
single-mindedly

seeking deliverance, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize non-arising, to broadly save sentient beings, to uphold and carry forward the Three Jewels, and to vow to repay the four kinds of kindness. With sincerity such as this, one's merit is not wasted, and one will surely gain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.)
(The Collection of Myriad Good Deeds Returning to the One)

[The wheel of suffering] The bitter fruits of birth and death turn like a wheel that never stops. [Non-arising] Beyond arising and ceasing—that is, the principle of nirvana. [Upholding and carrying forward] To inherit and develop. [The four kinds of kindness] The kindness of parents, of sentient beings (society), of the country and land, and of the Three Jewels. [Sincerity] Earnest and single-minded.
Therefore, single-mindedness means concentrating the mind on one thing, without a second thought.
The opposite of ‘single-mindedness’ is ‘a scattered mind.’
Master Hanshan teaches:
Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered—even if one shouts until the throat splits, it is all in vain.”
(See in detail
the Annotated Verses on Idle Wasted Effort

‘Single-mindedness’ is a very important basic concept of the Pure Land school. When reading the sutras and treatises, one must firmly grasp its meaning, or else a difference of a hair's breadth will lead to an error of a thousand miles.
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, in the Treatise on Rebirth, says:
“The mind constantly makes vows,
single-mindedly and without distraction recites the name,
thus ultimately attaining rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss, desiring
to practice samatha truly
for that reason.”
[Samatha] The translation is ‘cessation.’ Cessation means
the stilling of all scattered thoughts.

Editor's note: Originally, the meaning of ‘single-mindedness’ was simply to concentrate the mind on one thing, without a second thought. Since ancient times this has been the shared understanding of those who study the Buddha's teachings and the common knowledge of the Buddhist community; there has never been a second interpretation. But in recent years, because of the rampant spread of the Original Vow teaching, they have distorted ‘single-mindedness’ into ‘free of doubt and free of mixing’ (not doubting, and not practicing mixed with other methods), causing great confusion. Therefore, this is clarified here.
Single-minded recitation of the name is supremely excellent.
For if one recites the name single-mindedly, then the three trainings—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—are all complete:

Precepts guard against wrongdoing: if one can recite the name single-mindedly, then no evil can enter, and this is precepts. Concentration removes distraction: if one recites the name single-mindedly, the mind does not reach out to anything else, and this is concentration. Wisdom is clear illumination: if in contemplating the Buddha's name one makes each character clearly distinct, and also sees that the one who recites and the name that is recited are both unobtainable, then this is wisdom. Therefore single-minded recitation of the name is precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

[The three trainings] The training in precepts, the training in concentration, and the training in wisdom. Precepts are the prohibitions taught in the collection of monastic rules (the Vinaya), which prevent people from committing all evil deeds of body, speech, and mind. Concentration is meditative calm taught in the collection of sutras, which enables people to still their thoughts and clarify the mind. Wisdom is insight taught in the collection of treatises, which enables people to perceive the truth and cut off ignorance. Cultivating these three trainings, one can reach concentration through precepts, develop wisdom through concentration, and ultimately attain the undefiled fruit of the path; hence the three trainings are also called the ‘three undefiled trainings.’ [Undefiled] Pure and free of afflictions. ‘Outflow’ is another name for afflictions.
For if one recites the name single-mindedly, then the six perfections
(the six paramitas)
and all practices are complete:

Reciting the name single-mindedly, the myriad conditions are naturally let go—this is the perfection of giving. Reciting the name single-mindedly, all evil naturally ceases—this is the perfection of precepts. Reciting the name single-mindedly, the mind naturally becomes gentle—this is the perfection of patience. Reciting the name single-mindedly, one never regresses—this is the perfection of vigor. Reciting the name single-mindedly, no other thoughts arise—this is the perfection of meditation (dhyana). Reciting the name single-mindedly, right mindfulness is clear and distinct—this is the perfection of prajna (wisdom). Extending this to all practices, reciting the name single-mindedly fulfills all practices.

[The six perfections] The six methods of crossing from this shore of birth, death, and suffering to the far shore of nirvanic peace and bliss, namely: giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajna. Giving crosses over miserliness, precepts cross over transgression, patience crosses over anger, vigor crosses over indolence, meditation crosses over distraction, and prajna crosses over ignorance. [The six perfections and myriad practices] The Treatise on the Mind of Enlightenment says:
“After again passing through three asamkhyeya kalpas
(three great asamkhyeya kalpas)
and cultivating the six perfections and the myriad practices, all completely fulfilled, one then attains the fruit of Buddhahood.”

Therefore, single-minded recitation of the name is the great practice of peace and bliss and of great liberation. Letting go of the myriad conditions and reciting the name single-mindedly, one attains great freedom.
Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, teaches:
With single-minded attention
exclusively recollect the name of Amitabha Buddha, in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long,
never relinquishing it thought after thought
(with no thought drawn away by delusion)
— this is called
the practice of right concentration,
for it accords with the vow
of that Buddha
(Amitabha Buddha)
Now, Master Shandao's
regarding
single-minded recitation of the name
” teaching is annotated as follows

There are two kinds of practice: the first is correct practice; the second is mixed practice. By ‘correct practice’ is meant practicing exclusively in accordance with the scriptures on rebirth—this is called correct practice. What is this? With
single-minded attention
exclusively recite this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, the Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so on,
with single-minded attention
exclusively contemplate, observe, and recollect the two kinds of adornment of that land. If one worships, then
with single-minded attention
exclusively worship that Buddha; if one recites aloud, then
with single-minded attention
exclusively recite that Buddha; if one praises and makes offerings, then
with single-minded attention
exclusively praise and make offerings. This is called correct practice.]

Now, there are two kinds of practice: the first is correct practice; the second is mixed practice. Correct practice means practicing exclusively in accordance with the practice taught in the scriptures on rebirth—this is called correct practice. Which are correct practices? With single-minded and focused attention, to recite the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Amitabha Sutra, the Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so on; with single-minded and focused attention, to think upon, observe, and recollect the primary and dependent adornments of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. If one worships the Buddha, to worship Amitabha Buddha single-mindedly and with focused attention; if one recites aloud, to recite the name of Amitabha Buddha single-mindedly and with focused attention; if one praises and makes offerings, to praise and make offerings single-mindedly and with focused attention. This is called correct practice.

[The scriptures on rebirth] These are the three Pure Land sutras: the Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and the Amitabha Sutra. [The initial word yan] Here the ‘yan’ is a sentence-initial particle with no meaning. For example, in the phrase ‘yan gui yu hao’ it means ‘gui yu hao’ (that is, to be reconciled and to be on good terms with each other again).

[The two kinds of adornment] The adornments of the primary and dependent retributions. [Primary and dependent] The dependent retribution and the primary retribution. The dependent retribution is the reward in which one abides, such as the land, the earth, the houses, and the furnishings—that is, the living environment. The primary retribution is the body and mind of the Buddha and of sentient beings, which is the essential retributive body drawn forth by one's past karmic causes. The primary retribution of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is twofold: first, the adornment of the master, namely Amitabha Buddha; second, the adornment of the holy assembly, namely the bodhisattvas, sravakas, and devas of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. (See in detail the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.)
[Moreover, within these correct practices there are further two kinds: the first is
with single-minded attention
exclusively to recollect the name of Amitabha Buddha,
in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long,
never relinquishing it thought after thought
this is called
the practice of right concentration,
for it accords with the vow of that Buddha;

if one instead relies on worship, recitation, and so forth, these are called auxiliary practices. Apart from these two—correct and auxiliary—all other good deeds are called mixed practices. If one cultivates the aforementioned correct and auxiliary practices, the mind constantly draws near and recollects without break—this is called unbroken practice.]

Moreover, within these correct practices there are again two kinds: the first is single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting the name of Amitabha Buddha, in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long, never relinquishing it thought after thought—this is called the practice of right concentration, for it accords with the vow of Amitabha Buddha; if one instead relies on worship, praise, offerings, and so forth, these are called auxiliary practices. Apart from these two—correct and auxiliary—all other good deeds are called mixed practices. If one cultivates these correct and auxiliary practices, the mind constantly draws near to Amitabha Buddha and recollects without breaking—this is unbroken practice (with no deluded thoughts intruding)!
never relinquishing it thought after thought

] Each thought is the name of Amitabha Buddha. [Right concentration] Correct meditative concentration. When body and mind are pure and not scattered, it is called ‘right concentration.’ [Karma] The activity of body, speech, and mind. [For it accords with the vow of that Buddha] ‘With single-minded attention exclusively recollect the name of Amitabha Buddha, in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long, never relinquishing it thought after thought’—this is because it accords with the vow of Amitabha Buddha.
Master Shandao is an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha; his words are the words of Amitabha Buddha. From this it can be known that sentient beings
reciting the Buddha's name single-mindedly and never relinquishing it thought after thought
— this accords with the vow of the Buddha (Amitabha Buddha). Then,
reciting with a scattered mind goes against the Buddha's vow!
[Reciting with a scattered mind] Reciting the Buddha's name with the mouth while the mind thinks of other things.
Concerning recitation with a scattered mind,
Master Hanshan, in the Verses on Idle Wasted Effort, teaches:
Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered—even if one shouts until the throat splits, it is all in vain.”
[The Verses on Idle Wasted Effort] ‘

fei’ means to spend time and energy; ‘xian’ means useless, wasting effort. ‘Idle wasted effort’ is spending time and energy without achieving any real result—what is commonly called doing useless work. In the Verses on Idle Wasted Effort, Master Hanshan points out the common pitfalls of wasted effort in practice and how to emerge from them.
(See in detail
the Annotated Verses on Idle Wasted Effort
Now, I transcribe and annotate Master Hanshan's teaching—‘Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered, even if one shouts until the throat splits, it is all in vain’—as follows:

[To recite the Buddha's name is easy; the difficult thing is faith. When heart and mouth are not in accord, all is in vain. Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered—even if one shouts until the throat splits, it is all in vain.]

Reciting the Buddha's name is easy, but a sincere and truthful heart is hard. When heart and mouth are not in accord (the heart not being truthful: the mouth recites the Buddha's name while the mind thinks of other things), all is in vain (it is all wasted effort); reciting Amitabha Buddha with the mouth while the mind thinks of other things—even if one shouts until the throat splits, it counts for nothing.

[Faith] A sincere and truthful heart. When heart and mouth are not in accord, that is false. Hence the next line is ‘when heart and mouth are not in accord, all is in vain’ (that is, all wasted effort). The ‘faith’ here is not the faith of faith, vow, and practice, but the sense of being truthful and sincere. For example, the ‘trade wind’ (xin feng) is the wind that comes at the appointed time each year once a certain season arrives—a truthful wind. [Truthful] Meaning honest, without deceit. [Even if one shouts until the throat splits, it is all in vain] Because ‘reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered’ (reciting with a scattered mind) cannot accomplish the ten consecutive thoughts at the moment of death (this is the minimum requirement for rebirth; see in detail
the Conditions for Rebirth
), therefore one does not attain rebirth and all effort is wasted.
Here Master Hanshan points this out with piercing directness:
“Reciting Amitabha with the mouth while the mind is scattered
(that is, reciting with a scattered mind)
, even if one shouts until the throat splits, it is all in vain.”
Precisely because reciting the name is easy,
unbroken thought brings rebirth.
If one can
continue thought after thought without break,
making this the goal to the end of life,
then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.
May all people ponder this well. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
rouse the mind and restrain oneself
never desisting day or night.
When the last thought ends at the moment of death, the next thought is immediately reborn.
One will forever enjoy the dharma-joy of the unconditioned, and all the way to Buddhahood—how could this not be joyful!
[Unbroken] The thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name are joined together and not interrupted by deluded thoughts.
The following teaching is taken from Master Shandao's ‘On the Correct and Mixed Practices of Pure Karma,’
and tells specifically how reciting the Buddha's name brings rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Master Yinguang, the manifestation of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva,
greatly admired this teaching and praised it, saying:

“The Elder Shandao is an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha; he possesses great spiritual powers and great wisdom. In his grand exposition of the Pure Land, he does not prize the mysterious and sublime, but only teaches people to practice in a genuine, truthful, and plain manner.
As for the ‘Correct and Mixed Practices’ that he sets forth, its benefit is limitless.
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, the Letter in Reply to the Yongjia Lay Brothers)

[Question: Why did he not have them practice contemplation, but directly instruct them to exclusively recite the name? Answer: Sentient beings are heavily burdened with obstacles; the object (to be contemplated) is subtle while the mind is coarse, the consciousness is restless and the spirit flies, so contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage
(Sakyamuni Buddha)
out of compassion, directly urged exclusively reciting the name. Precisely because reciting the name is easy,
unbroken thought brings rebirth.
If one can
continue thought after thought without break,
make this the goal throughout life
that is, one who practices thus for life

, of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. Why is this? Because there are no external distracting conditions, one gains right mindfulness, one accords with the Buddha's fundamental vow, one does not go against the teaching, and one complies with the Buddha's words.]

Question: Why did Sakyamuni Buddha, in the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, not have them practice contemplation (referring to the thirteen contemplations in the sutra, such as the contemplation of the sun and the contemplation of water), but directly taught them to exclusively recite the name? Answer: Sentient beings have deep and heavy karmic obstacles; the object (the realm to be contemplated) is subtle while the mind is coarse, the consciousness is restless and the spirit flies, so contemplation is difficult to accomplish. Therefore Sakyamuni Buddha, in his compassion, directly taught them to exclusively recite the name of Amitabha Buddha.
It is precisely because reciting the name—being easier to accomplish than contemplation
that when one approaches death, as long as one's thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name continue unbroken
(not interrupted by deluded thoughts),
one thereupon attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

If one can keep the thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name unbroken and practice thus for life, then of ten people, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. Why? Because in exclusively reciting the name the mind does not reach out (the mind does not reach out here and there to various external conditions) and thereby gains right mindfulness; because it accords with Amitabha Buddha's fundamental vow; because it does not go against the teaching of Sakyamuni Buddha; and because it complies with the sacred words of Sakyamuni Buddha.
[Unbroken thought brings rebirth]
‘Unbroken thought brings rebirth’ means:
at the moment of death, when the thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name are unbroken
(not interrupted by deluded thoughts),
one thereupon attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Here ‘unbroken’ means the thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name following one after another, with no deluded thoughts mixed in between (if deluded thoughts are mixed in, it is not unbroken). One must not misunderstand the two characters ‘unbroken’ here as the unbroken out-loud recitation of the name (while the mind is mixed with deluded thoughts). As the saying goes, a difference of a hair's breadth leads to an error of a thousand miles. [Continuing thought after thought, making this the goal to the end of life] Because, at the moment of death, unbroken thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name bring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one should therefore practice thus for life,
so that the thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name become unbroken and, through repeated practice, become second nature.

Then one will surely attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss—of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. [Becoming second nature through repeated practice] Through repeated and uninterrupted practice, the continuing thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name become a natural instinct.

Question: How do we know that ‘unbroken thought brings rebirth’ means that at the moment of death, unbroken thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name bring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and not that in daily life, as long as one has at some point continued thought after thought, one will thereby be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at death?
Answer: Master Shandao teaches:
“If one can continue thought after thought,
making this the goal to the end of life
(that is, one who practices thus for life)
, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.”
Please note that it says
‘one who makes this the goal to the end of life,’
and not someone who merely continued thought after thought at some time in daily life. Master Shandao continues his teaching:
“May all people ponder this well. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself and never desist day or night,
so that when the last thought ends at the moment of death, the next thought is immediately reborn.
Then one will forever enjoy the dharma-joy of the unconditioned, and all the way to Buddhahood—how could this not be joyful!”
Therefore, ‘unbroken thought brings rebirth’ means that at the moment of death, unbroken thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name bring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Question: How do we know that ‘unbroken’ in ‘unbroken thought brings rebirth’ means ‘the thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name are unbroken,’ and not ‘the name is recited out loud without break (while the mind is mixed with deluded thoughts)’?
Answer: The answer is found in detail in
this Study Garden
‘Master Shandao: Unbroken Thought Brings Rebirth’
The supreme excellence of unbroken recitation of the Buddha's name—
Master Shandao, in the Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra, teaches:
If one is able to recite the Buddha's name unbrokenly,
that person is exceedingly rare, and there is nothing that can be compared to him
(nothing can be set beside it)
; therefore the pundarika is cited as a simile
(that is, the pundarika flower is used as an illustration).

The pundarika is called the good flower among men, also called the rare flower, the supreme among men, and the most exquisite flower among men. This flower is traditionally called the ‘cai’ flower; just so, one who recites the Buddha's name
(that is, one who thus recites the Buddha's name)
is a good person among men, a most exquisite good person among men, a supreme person among men, a rare person among men, and the most excellent person among men.”

[If one abandons single-minded recitation and practices mixed karma, then of a hundred one will rarely get one or two; of a thousand, rarely three or four. Why? Because of being stirred by miscellaneous conditions and losing right mindfulness; because one does not accord with the Buddha's fundamental vow; because one goes against the teaching; because one does not comply with the Buddha's words;
because one's bound recollection is not unbroken;

because one's mind, not continuing, does not recollect to repay the Buddha's kindness; because, though one performs karmic practices, they constantly accord with fame and profit; and because one delights in drawing near to miscellaneous conditions, oneself obstructing and obstructing others from the correct practice of rebirth.]

If one abandons single-minded and exclusive recitation of the name of Amitabha Buddha and practices mixed karma, then of a hundred people barely one or two attain rebirth; of a thousand, barely three or four. Why? Because the mind reaches out here and there, losing right mindfulness; because one does not accord with Amitabha Buddha's fundamental vow; because one goes against the teaching of Sakyamuni Buddha; because one does not comply with the sacred words of Sakyamuni Buddha; because one's bound recollection is not unbroken; because the mind, not continuing, does not recollect so as to repay the Buddha's kindness; because, though one performs all kinds of karmic practices, they constantly accord with fame and profit; and because one delights in drawing near to miscellaneous conditions, oneself obstructing (obstructing oneself) and obstructing others (obstructing others) from the correct practice of rebirth.

[May all people ponder this well. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, never desisting day or night. When the last thought ends at the moment of death, the next thought is immediately reborn. One will forever enjoy the dharma-joy of the unconditioned, and all the way to Buddhahood—how could this not be joyful!]
May
all people
ponder this well. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
all
must
rouse themselves and restrain themselves,
, never desisting day or night from the unbroken thought-after-thought recitation.
Practicing thus,
when the last thought ends at the moment of death, the next thought is immediately reborn
in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
One will forever enjoy the dharma-joy of the unconditioned, and all the way to Buddhahood—how could this not be joyful!

[Rousing the mind and restraining oneself] ‘Rousing the mind’ means rousing one's mind to do what ought to be done; ‘restraining oneself’ means restraining oneself from doing what ought not to be done. The four characters ‘rouse the mind and restrain oneself’ are a powerful weapon for overcoming difficulties and removing obstacles.
[Never desisting day or night] Do not stop day or night from the unbroken thought-after-thought recitation.

[When the last thought ends, the next thought is immediately reborn] This means: because the thoughts of reciting the Buddha's name are unbroken, the final thought at the moment of death must be a thought of reciting the Buddha's name;
and immediately after that final thought
one is reborn at once in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Question: The teaching of Master Shandao on how to attain rebirth (

“Precisely because reciting the name is easy, unbroken thought brings rebirth. If one can continue thought after thought, making this the goal to the end of life, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.

May all people ponder this well. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself and never desist day or night, so that when the last thought ends at the moment of death, the next thought is immediately reborn.
One will forever enjoy the dharma-joy of the unconditioned, and all the way to Buddhahood—how could this not be joyful!”
) — what is its relationship to faith and vow?

Answer: In this teaching, faith and vow are both complete. For only through deep faith and an earnest vow can one accomplish ‘continuing thought after thought, making this the goal to the end of life’ and ‘rousing the mind and restraining oneself, never desisting day or night’; and ‘continuing thought after thought, making this the goal to the end of life’ and ‘rousing the mind and restraining oneself, never desisting day or night’ are likewise the concrete expression and the test of deep faith and an earnest vow.
Question: The teaching of Master Shandao on how to attain rebirth (

“Precisely because reciting the name is easy, unbroken thought brings rebirth. If one can continue thought after thought, making this the goal to the end of life, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.

May all people ponder this well. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself and never desist day or night, so that when the last thought ends at the moment of death, the next thought is immediately reborn.
One will forever enjoy the dharma-joy of the unconditioned, and all the way to Buddhahood—how could this not be joyful!”
) — what is its relationship to ‘the ten consecutive thoughts at the moment of death, and unbroken thought brings rebirth’?
Answer: This teaching includes ‘the ten consecutive thoughts at the moment of death, and unbroken thought brings rebirth.’ Moreover, Master Shandao has a teaching concerning
‘the ten consecutive thoughts at the moment of death, and unbroken thought brings rebirth’
, such as:

If I attain Buddhahood, and all sentient beings in the ten directions recite my name and aspire to be reborn in my land—even down to ten thoughts—and if they are not reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
(The Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra)

If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings of the ten directions, who wish to be reborn in my land, call upon my name even as few as ten times, and yet are not reborn through the power of my vow, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
(from the Contemplation of the Dharma-gate)
If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings of the ten directions call upon my name even as few as ten times, and yet are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
from the Praise of Rebirth)
The “as few as ten thoughts” and “as few as ten voices” spoken of here, taken together with what Master Shandao instructed above —
“Precisely because recitation of the name is easy, unbroken thought brings rebirth. If one can
continue thought after thought to the end of life
, then of ten, ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn”
—make it clear that this is an abbreviated way of saying “for a whole life span, thought after thought continuing, and at the very least,
the ten unbroken thoughts at the moment of death
,” for Master Shandao has already said plainly:
“Thought after thought continuing, to the end of life.”
And
“Thought after thought continuing, to the end of life”
is precisely in order to make thought-after-thought continuing a firmly formed habit,
so as to ensure the ten unbroken thoughts at the moment of death
If, at the moment of death, one does not recitate, or recitates with a scattered mind, then one has not fulfilled
“thought after thought continuing, to the end of life”
Therefore,
“down to ten thoughts, and if not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”
means precisely this:
the ten unbroken thoughts at the moment of death bring immediate rebirth.
[Ten thoughts, ten voices] Reciting the Buddha’s name for ten thought-moments.
[Thought after thought continuing, formed into a habit] Through constant repeated practice, making thought-after-thought continuing a natural instinct.
Note:
The “down to ten thoughts (ten voices)” taught by Master Shandao is without any doubt the ten thoughts of continuous recitation at the moment of death, for this is
right mindfulness at the moment of death

. Yet in recent years, through the inroads of the Primal Vow teaching, right and wrong have become confounded, and two other interpretations have appeared: first, that “down to ten thoughts (ten voices)” means having recited the Buddha’s name at least ten times, so that anyone who has ever recited it ten times in daily life will certainly be reborn — this is the theoretical basis for “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth”; second, that “down to ten thoughts (ten voices)” means ten thoughts of scattered-mind recitation at the moment of death — this is the theoretical basis for the claim that scattered-mind recitation also brings certain rebirth. Both interpretations are erroneous. For
if
one has
merely recited the Buddha’s name ten times in daily life but
does not recitate at the moment of death, or, though recitating, recitates with a scattered mind, neither case fulfills
“thought after thought continuing, to the end of life”
Therefore
“down to ten thoughts (ten voices)”
means at the very least
the ten thoughts of continuous recitation at the moment of death
. Hence Master Daochuo instructed clearly:
If there be sentient beings who, even having committed evil all their lives, at the moment of death
recite for ten thoughts without break
, calling upon my name,
and are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
(from the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove)

blocks.text: 3. Right Mindfulness at the Moment of Death

inline.s: Whether rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss requires right mindfulness at the moment of death
is the watershed that divides the orthodox teaching of the Pure Land school from heretical views
. Orthodox teaching follows the scriptures and affirms that right mindfulness at death is required; hence Master Shandao instructed:
“Unbroken thought brings rebirth.”
Master Yongming instructed:
“The ten thoughts at the moment of death are accomplished.”
Master Lianchi instructed:
“Within, right mindfulness gathers; without, the Buddha comes to welcome.”
Master Yinguang instructed:

“All who recitate the Buddha’s name should give rise to the great bodhi-mind of universally saving sentient beings; then the circumstances of this present life will be smooth, and with right mindfulness at death they will be reborn. From this they depart from the stream of ordinary beings and join the ranks of sages and worthies; relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power and their own vow, they turn back into the Saha world, manifesting all manner of forms to liberate sentient beings.”
The patriarchs of the Pure Land school have likewise taught again and again:
rebirth through right mindfulness at the moment of death.
(See further
“Right Mindfulness at Death”
, in the article)

But the heretical doctrine of the Primal Vow teaching violates the scriptures and denies the need for right mindfulness at death, proclaiming that recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth, that one need not observe precepts, need not cultivate merit, need not purify one’s own mind — and that even committing evil throughout one’s life is of no consequence.
[Purify one’s own mind] From the admonition-verse shared by the seven Buddhas:
“Refrain from all evil, practice all good, purify your own mind — this is the teaching of all Buddhas.”

The seven Buddhas of the past all took this verse as the principle of their precept practice, so it is called the “admonition-verse shared by the seven Buddhas.” The heretical doctrine of the Primal Vow teaching urges that “one need not observe precepts,” which is to deny “refrain from all evil”; “one need not cultivate merit,” which is to deny “practice all good”; and furthermore one need not “purify one’s own mind.” Can this still be called Buddhism? [Seven Buddhas] The seven Buddhas of the past, namely Vipasyin, Sikhin, Visvabhu, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kasyapa, and Sakyamuni Buddha.
Moreover, in the Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao explained the meaning of the section on “the lowest grade, the lowest birth”:

“From ‘such a foolish person’ down to ‘the offense of birth-and-death,’ it clearly sets forth the benefits gained in this very life through hearing the Dharma and reciting the Buddha’s name; there are ten points: first, it again identifies the person who has committed evil; second, it shows that his life has little time remaining; third, it shows that at death he meets a good spiritual friend; fourth, it shows that the good person comforts and instructs him to recitate the Buddha’s name; fifth, it shows that the pains of death press upon the offender so that he cannot of himself recite the name; sixth, it shows that the good friend, knowing his suffering and lost mindfulness, turns to teach him to call aloud the name of Amitabha; seventh, it shows how many recitations there are, voice after voice without interruption; eighth, it shows the removal of offenses of many kalpas; ninth, it shows that
with right mindfulness at death
, a golden lotus forthwith arrives to respond; tenth, it shows the swiftness or slowness of departure, until he reaches the land of his destination.”
Please note especially that here Master Shandao says:
rebirth through right mindfulness at death
(“with right mindfulness at death, a golden lotus forthwith arrives to respond”). (See further
“Commentary on the Lowest Grade, Lowest Birth Section of the Contemplation Sutra”
, in the article.) Yet the Primal Vow teaching, which loudly claims to “rely upon Master Shandao,” firmly opposes rebirth through right mindfulness at death
— is this, then, how one relies upon him?!
For more on right mindfulness at death, please refer to
“Right Mindfulness at Death”
and
“Right Mindfulness at Death: Answers to a Guest’s Questions”
, in these two articles.
The following instruction is taken from Master Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness and Rebirth at Death (see further
“Master Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness and Rebirth at Death (Annotated)”
[If, at the approach of the end of a grave illness, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor raise sounds of sighing and regret, which would disturb the patient’s mind and
cause him to lose right mindfulness

. Let them recite the Buddha’s name together with one voice; only when the breath has ceased may they weep. If there is the least attachment to this world in his heart, it becomes an obstruction, and he cannot be liberated. If there is someone who understands the Pure Land, and comes often to encourage him, that is a great fortune. If one does according to this, he will certainly be reborn beyond, without doubt.]

If, when a grave illness approaches the end of life, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor raise sounds of sighing and regret, lest they disturb the patient’s mind and spirit and make him lose right mindfulness. They must recite the Buddha’s name with one voice, and only after the patient’s breath has ceased may they weep. For if the patient has the least attachment to this world, it becomes an obstruction to rebirth, and he cannot be liberated. If there is someone who understands the Pure Land and comes often to encourage him, this is most fortunate. If one acts according to this, the patient will certainly and without doubt be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

This method — practiced by monks, laypeople, and those who have never recitated, — all are reborn, without any doubt. I have seen many in the world who, in ordinary daily life, recitate the Buddha’s name, praise and bow, and make vows to be reborn in the West, with great
earnestness and sincerity

. Yet when they come to be ill, they are afraid of death, and speak no more of rebirth and liberation. Only when their breath has faded and life has ended, and their consciousness has entered the dark realm, do they at last begin to recitate and strike the bell. This is exactly like closing the door after the thief has gone — of what use is it? Birth and death are a great matter;
one must exert one’s own strength
to succeed.
If there be a single thought-moment of error
(if the final thought at death is a deluded thought rather than right mindfulness)
, and one suffers for many kalpas
, who can take your place?
Think on this! Think on this!
When one is free of illness, one should earnestly take up and hold this method — this is the great matter of the final hour.]

This “method of right mindfulness and rebirth at death” (the patient must do his utmost to maintain right mindfulness at death; the relatives must not weep or lament lest they disturb the patient’s right mindfulness; and a good spiritual friend’s timely guidance and encouragement can help the patient arouse and sustain right mindfulness at death) — practiced by monks, laypeople, and those who have never recitated, — all are reborn, with no doubt whatever. I have seen many in the world who, in ordinary daily life, recitate the Buddha’s name, praise and bow, and vow to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, most earnestly and sincerely. Yet when illness comes, they are afraid of death and speak no more of rebirth and liberation. Only when their own breath has faded and life ended, and their consciousness has been cast into the dark realm, do they at last recitate and strike the bell. This is exactly like closing the door after the thief has gone (it is too late to shut the door against theft after the thief has already taken the goods) — of what use is it? Birth and death are a great matter;
one must diligently apply one’s own effort
to succeed.
If the final thought at death be one thought in error
(if the thought at death be a deluded thought rather than right mindfulness)
, the consequence is suffering for many kalpas
, who can take your place?
You must weigh this well! Weigh it well!

Before sickness comes, one should earnestly take up and hold this “method of right mindfulness and rebirth at death” (one should make full preparation for right mindfulness at death in advance — that is what Master Yongming calls “preparing the ferry and the bridge” — and at the same time instruct the relatives that they must not weep or lament; having a good spiritual friend’s help at the final hour is even better). This is the great matter of the final hour!

Question: The Primal Vow teaching claims that “the gate of the Grand Vow,” “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth,” and “the evil person as the proper object [of salvation]” are the Pure Land thought of Master Shandao. Is this so?
Answer: This is a complete distortion and slander of Master Shandao’s Pure Land thought! The gate of the Grand Vow was fabricated by Master Honen — see further
“Master Honen’s Fabrication of the Gate of the Grand Vow”
, in that article
. “Recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth” was likewise fabricated by Master Honen, Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and others! (See further
“Does Recitation of the Name Necessarily Bring Rebirth?”
, in that article.) Master Shandao never said “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth.” On the contrary, Master Shandao said:
“Unbroken thought brings rebirth”
and “rebirth through right mindfulness at death”

. As for the slander that Master Shandao taught “the evil person as the proper object [of salvation],” one has only to look at what Master Shandao instructed in the Commentary in Four Fascicles on the Contemplation Sutra to know the truth of the matter. Master Shandao said:
“Sincere means genuine; truthful means real. To make clear that the understanding and practice cultivated by the body, speech, and mind karma of all sentient beings
must be done from a mind that is truly real
one must not outwardly display the appearance of virtue and diligence while inwardly harboring falsity
, greed, anger, perversity, and deceit, with a hundred kinds of treachery — a nature so vicious that it is hard to be transformed, like serpents and scorpions. Though they produce the three karmas
(of body, speech, and mind)

, this is called “the virtue mixed with poison,” also called “false practice,” and is not real karma. If one settles the mind and practices in this way, though he torment his body and mind, day and night through all twelve periods, rushing and toiling as if his head were on fire, this is all
(a general term for ‘altogether’)
called “the virtue mixed with poison.”
He who wishes to turn this practice mixed with poison around and seek rebirth in the Buddha’s Pure Land
can surely not attain it.”
Master Shandao points out that these evil persons inwardly harboring falsity (and persons such as Honen belong to this class)
“seek rebirth in the Buddha’s Pure Land — this surely cannot be attained”
how can it be said that the salvation of Amitabha takes the evil person as its proper object? (For the refutation of “the evil person as the proper object,” see further
“The Primal Vow Teaching Is an Outwardly-Buddhist Heresy”
, in that article.)

The Buddha-recitation practice has four methods of recitation: first, recitation of the name — single-mindedly calling upon the Buddha’s name; second, recitation before an image — contemplating the Buddha’s image while calling his name; third, recitation by visualization — single-mindedly contemplating the auspicious marks and adornments of the Buddha; fourth, recitation of true reality — single-mindedly contemplating the real Dharmakaya of the Buddha. Among these four methods, which best accords with the capacities of sentient beings, with great merit and easy practice, with little effort and swift effect? Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, made a clear decision for us and chose the method most suited to the capacity of the Dharma-ending age — recitation of the name. In the Practice of Specialized and Miscellaneous Cultivation, Master Shandao instructed:

“Sentient beings have heavy obstructions; the realm is subtle while the mind is coarse, consciousness floats and the spirit flies — so visual contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage
(Sakyamuni Buddha)
in compassion
directly urged
exclusive recitation of the name
Precisely because recitation of the name is easy,
unbroken thought brings rebirth

(Translation: sentient beings have heavy karmic obstructions; the realm (the object contemplated) is subtle while the mind is coarse, consciousness floats and the spirit flies, so visual-contemplation recitation is hard to accomplish. Therefore Sakyamuni Buddha, in compassion, directly taught them the recitation of the name — to call exclusively upon the name of Amitabha Buddha. Precisely because recitation of the name is easier than visualization, at the moment of death, one need only keep the mindful thought unbroken, and he will be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.)
Once the great direction is set — that the cultivation of the Pure Land school should devote itself to recitation of the name (
“exclusively call upon the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth”
) — the question that immediately follows is: how are we to ensure
that the mindful thought is unbroken at the moment of death
? Therefore Master Shandao went on to instruct:
“If one can
continue thought after thought to the end of life
one who
(a person who practices thus his whole life)
, then of ten, ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn......May all people reflect well within themselves: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing
; when the final thought ends life, the next thought forthwith brings rebirth; forever enjoying unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and on to Buddhahood — how joyful!”

[Thought after thought continuing, to the end of life] Because, at the moment of death, unbroken mindful thought brings immediate rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one should thus practice for one’s whole life, making thought-after-thought continuing a firmly formed habit. Then one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss — of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.
In this instruction, Master Shandao teaches:
“Exclusively call upon the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth.”
And,
in order to accomplish unbroken thought bringing rebirth at the moment of death, one must
“continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing”
, making thought-after-thought continuing a firmly formed habit. Thus the program of practice of the Pure Land school is established:
call exclusively upon the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth; continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing.

This thoroughly and completely resolves the fundamental issue of Pure Land practice: which method of recitation to adopt? How to recitate? — in order to ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss!

The “exclusive recitation of the name” of which Master Shandao speaks here is the exclusive recitation of the name that continues thought after thought — that is, what he earlier taught as “single-mindedly invoking the name of Amitabha Buddha,” namely single-minded recitation of the name. Hence “call exclusively upon the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth; continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing” can be expressed as:
Single-mindedly recite the name; unbroken thought brings rebirth. Continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing.
These twenty-four
great characters
are the golden highroad to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss
the program of practice of the Pure Land school, the wondrous method that ensures rebirth,
the very essence of Master Shandao’s Pure Land teaching. Those who practice thus
—of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn, forever enjoying unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and on to Buddhahood — how joyful!
On this, Master Yinguang instructed:

“The method of reciting the Buddha’s name is about four: recitation of the name, recitation before an image, recitation by visualization, and recitation of true reality. Among these four, only recitation of the name gathers the widest capacities, is the easiest to begin, and does not give rise to demonic obstructions.

Master Shandao said: ‘Sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age have floating consciousness, coarse minds and subtle realms, so visualization is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage in compassion
especially urged
exclusive recitation of the name
because recitation of the name is easy,
unbroken thought brings rebirth
’ I truly fear that some may not apply their minds well and so fall into a demonic state.”
(from the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang
Reply to Layman Wu Xizhen, First Letter)
Continue thought after thought to the end of life; rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing
” — this is the key to the accomplishment of name-recitation, and we must unfailingly follow it. All study and all teaching likewise should revolve around this core, so as to ensure rebirth.

Conversely, if one recitates “without a mind of thought-after-thought continuity, and with a will to break off again and again,” relying upon this negligent practice, then to hope for rebirth at the final hour is difficult — for the present is the cause and the final hour the fruit. This is [spoken by] the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha
Master Yongming instructed:
“If speech and conduct do not match
(if what one says and what one does are not in accord)
, with weak strength of faith, without a mind of thought-after-thought continuity, and a will to break off again and again
(the mindful thought of recitation broken off by deluded thoughts)
relying
(trusting in)
this negligence, then at the final hour, hoping for rebirth, he is but obstructed by karmic hindrances, and in fear will be unable to meet his good friend
(for fear he will not meet a spiritual friend who can arouse his right mindfulness at death)
; the winds and fire press upon him, and right mindfulness is not accomplished. Why is this? For
the present is the cause and the final hour is the fruit

; so the cause must be real, and the fruit will then not be empty. If one wishes the ten thoughts at death to be accomplished, he should but prepare the ferry and the bridge in advance, gather together merit, and dedicate it to that hour, so that thought after thought is without lapse — then there is nothing to fear.”
(from the Collected Essays on the Common Return of All Good Deeds)
[The ten thoughts at the moment of death accomplished] Accomplishing the ten unbroken thoughts at the moment of death.
(See further
“The Ten Thoughts at Death: Unbroken Thought Brings Rebirth”
, in that article.)
[Preparing the ferry and the bridge] “Ferry and bridge”: a crossing and a bridge, that is, making preparation in advance.
Question: How can one accomplish “unbroken thought brings rebirth”?
Answer: Master Shandao instructed:
“May all people reflect well within themselves: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing
. When the final thought ends life, the next thought forthwith brings rebirth; forever enjoying unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and on to Buddhahood — how joyful!”
In this instruction,
the six characters “rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing”

are the essential secret of accomplishing “unbroken thought brings rebirth,” making thought-after-thought continuing a firmly formed habit. Thus, at the moment of death, one is able to keep thought after thought unbroken and be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. To this end, one must certainly firm up one’s resolve for the Way and, with tireless diligence, accomplish “rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing.” In today’s world, the sea of desire runs wild, people’s minds turn toward evil, and they are the more off the Way. Adding to this, false teachers fan the flames and invert the teaching, so that reciters of the Buddha’s name are immersed in an evil cauldron without precedent in history. To firm up one’s resolve for the Way and remain unstained by the mud, I advise you to take up the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching (see further
“Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching”

), recite it often and practice it, so as to withstand the disturbances from within and without and the invasions of material desire, and accomplish the work of the Way. As for the specific method of recitation, see
“Mindful Recitation”
. As long as you are earnest, diligent, hardworking, and persevering, you will certainly accomplish “unbroken thought brings rebirth.”
Question: How does one accomplish
“continue thought after thought
to the end of life”?
Answer:
The Avatamsaka Sutra says:
“Never forget the first resolve, and only then is the end attained.”
This means: never forget the original resolve, and only then can one carry through from beginning to end (persevere to the very end). That is,
never forgetting the original resolve, one can overcome all difficulties and, unbending, walk from the starting point to the goal. Hence the Avatamsaka Sutra also says:
“All the Tathagatas of the three times
(without exception)
protect and keep in mind the first resolve.”

For one who recites the Buddha’s name, one must always remember the original resolve to practice Buddhism so as to put an end to birth and death, and with unshakable perseverance, overcoming all difficulties, tirelessly accomplish “continue thought after thought to the end of life.”

When Buddhist practitioners first resolve to practice, they are all vigorous and diligent, advancing in both understanding and practice. But as time passes, some cannot bear the refining of practice and gradually lose the advancing mind of the Way they once had, becoming lax and indulgent; others simply give up, drifting with the world, and even falling into the trap of fame and profit. Facing the difficulty of practice, it is often said in the Buddhist community: “The first year a renunciant, the Buddha is in his heart; the second year, the Buddha is before his eyes; the third year, the Buddha is far off in the sky.” So those who practice Buddhism must
not forget the original resolve
and be as at the very first
, so as to accomplish the work of the Way.

Master Xuanzang’s journey to India to fetch the scriptures set a shining example of “never forget the first resolve, and only then is the end attained.” The Master left home at thirteen in the Jingtu Monastery at Luoyang, and thereafter traveled to various places, seeking out noted teachers. In the course of listening to the teachings, he was deeply troubled that the various explanations were in conflict and that he could find no resolution. In order to seek the true Dharma and set things in order at their source, he made the vow to travel west. In the first year of the Zhenguan era (
), when his request to the court for permission to travel west came to nothing, the Master set out privately from Chang’an with his fellow practitioners to seek the scriptures in the west.

The Master’s company first passed through Lanzhou and reached Liangzhou (Wuwei, Gansu). To avoid being questioned and searched along the way, they traveled by night and lay hidden by day. Then, passing through the Jade Gate Pass, crossing the Fiery Mountain, traversing thousands of li of the vast shifting sands, going through the uninhabited lands where vipers and wolves prowl, having tasted every hardship, they at last reached Yi-wu (Hami, Xinjiang). After a brief rest, the company pressed on and arrived at the kingdom of Gaochang (Turpan, Xinjiang). Then, crossing the Congling range and the Iron Gate, they reached the kingdom of Baktria (in the north of present-day Afghanistan), passed through the kingdom of Udyana (the Swat region of Pakistan), and arrived at the kingdom of Kashmir (northwestern India). After studying there for two years, Master Xuanzang pressed on again and, in the fifth year of the Zhenguan era (

), arrived at Nalanda monastery in the kingdom of Magadha, where he studied under Master Silabhadra, learning the doctrine of Consciousness-Only. Master Xuanzang studied at Nalanda for thirteen years, studying the scriptures and treatises of both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles, and gained the very essence of the Dharma.

In order to fulfill the original resolve he had made, Master Xuanzang, though he endured a thousand hardships and ten thousand difficulties on the road, and sometimes even peril to his life, never once retreated a half step. In particular, when crossing the great desert of the Mobei Sands between Lop Nur and the Jade Gate Pass, he encountered unimaginable difficulties. The Master’s biography describes it: “Above, no birds in flight; below, no roaming beasts; grass and trees do not grow, and the tracks of men are utterly rare; at times the wind rolls up sand and stones, at times the sun blazes down and the heat steams; at times he sees withered bones covering the plain, the remnants of battlefields; at times he sees fierce beasts and phantom shapes

By day, under the blazing sun, the temperature of the desert was extreme, and there was no place to set foot. The Master had no recourse but to bury himself in the sand and wait for night to continue his journey. In the boundless desert, the Master also once lost his way. Under such desperate circumstances, some of the company, unable to bear it, gave up the westward journey, and others died along the way. Master Xuanzang, never forgetting his original resolve, holding to the determination “I would rather take one step toward the West and die, than take half a step toward the East and live,” enduring hunger and thirst, his life hanging by a thread, at last reached Nalanda monastery in India, gained the very essence of the Dharma, and fully fulfilled his great vow to go west and seek the scriptures.
I would rather take one step toward the West and die, than take half a step toward the East and live.
In
concrete practice, Master Yinguang instructed:

“Whether at home or in a monastery, one must respect superiors and be kind to those below. Endure what others cannot endure; practice what others cannot practice. Take on others’ burdens and bring about others’ good. When sitting quietly, always reflect on one’s own faults; in idle conversation, never discuss others’ wrongs.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether dressing or eating, from morning to evening, from evening to morning, let a single phrase of the Buddha’s name not be interrupted. Recite in a low voice, or recite silently; apart from recitation, do not give rise to any other thought. If a deluded thought should arise, put an end to it on the spot.

Always give rise to a mind of shame and repentance. Even if you have cultivations, always feel that your own effort is shallow, and never boast. Look only after your own affairs, not those of others. Look only at good examples, not at bad ones. Regard all people as bodhisattvas, and think that I alone am truly an ordinary being. If you can truly practice according to what I have said, you will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.”
(from the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang, Third Compilation
Reply to Layman Ye Fubei, First Letter)

Furthermore, you may also adopt the method of reciting the Buddha’s name in accord with the breath, so as to form it into a habit, which makes it easier to accomplish “continue thought after thought to the end of life.” (See further
“Essentials of Breathing Recitation”
, in that article.)
